entries.topicDescription: Reactive streams built on coroutines for asynchronous data processing.

tips.title: Flow basics — cold async streams
tips.content:
Flow is Kotlin's answer to reactive streams. It's cold — the producer
code runs only when someone collects the flow.

Unlike channels or LiveData, flows are declarative pipelines.
You build a flow with the 'flow { }' builder and emit values with 'emit()'.

Flows integrate naturally with coroutines — they suspend instead of blocking,
and they're cancelled when the collecting coroutine is cancelled.

tips.title: StateFlow and SharedFlow
tips.content:
StateFlow is a hot flow that always holds a current value.
It replays the latest value to new collectors and ignores duplicate emissions.

SharedFlow is more flexible — configurable replay cache and buffer.
Use it for events that shouldn't be replayed (navigation, snackbar). With the default replay = 0, an event emitted while nobody is collecting is dropped — use a Channel (receiveAsFlow) when an event must never be lost.

StateFlow = state holder (replaces LiveData).
SharedFlow = event bus (one-shot events).
Both are hot — they exist independently of collectors.

tips.title: Flow operators — combine, flatMapLatest, debounce
tips.content:
Flow operators transform, combine, and control the timing of emissions.
They create new flows — the original flow is unchanged (immutable pipeline).

combine() merges multiple flows, emitting when any flow updates.
flatMapLatest() cancels the previous inner flow when a new value arrives.
debounce() waits for a pause in emissions before forwarding.

These operators are the building blocks of reactive UI patterns
like search-as-you-type and multi-source state combination.

tips.title: Use a suspend function for one value and a Flow for values over time
tips.content:
A suspend function returns a single result and then it is done: loading a profile, saving a form. A Flow represents a sequence of values that arrive over time: database changes, location updates, search results as the user types.

Choosing the wrong one causes awkward code. Returning a Flow for a one-shot call forces callers to collect it and then cancel it, and polling a suspend function in a loop reinvents what a Flow already gives you. A Room query that returns Flow<List<T>> is a good example: it emits again whenever the data changes.

tips.title: Operators are lazy; a terminal operator starts the flow
tips.content:
Intermediate operators like map, filter, take and onEach only describe a pipeline — nothing runs until a terminal operator is called. collect is the general one; first(), single(), toList() and reduce() collect and return a result. first() also cancels the upstream flow as soon as it has its value.

launchIn(scope) is a terminal operator that collects in a new coroutine and returns its Job, which is convenient in a ViewModel or a Fragment when you have several flows to observe and use onEach for the work.
tips.codeSnippet:
val source = flowOf(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

val doubled = source.map { it * 2 }      // nothing has run yet
val firstBig = doubled.first { it > 4 }  // 6, and the flow is cancelled after it
val all = doubled.toList()               // [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]

// Collect in a new coroutine without a nested launch
doubled
    .onEach { render(it) }
    .launchIn(viewModelScope)

tips.title: flowOn changes where upstream runs, never where the collector runs
tips.content:
A flow runs in the coroutine that collects it. To move expensive upstream work (disk, parsing) to another dispatcher, apply flowOn: it changes the context for everything above it, and the collector still runs in its own context. This is called context preservation, and it means a collector on the main thread can safely update the UI.

Don't call withContext inside flow { } to emit from another dispatcher — the flow throws an IllegalStateException because emissions must come from the collector's context. flowOn (or channelFlow) is the supported way.

tips.title: buffer, conflate and collectLatest for a slow collector
tips.content:
By default a flow is sequential: the producer emits the next value only after the collector finishes the previous one, so a slow collector slows the whole pipeline. Three tools change that.

buffer() lets the producer keep emitting into a buffer while the collector works. conflate() also runs concurrently but drops intermediate values, so the collector only sees the latest. collectLatest cancels the previous collector block when a new value arrives, which suits work whose result is obsolete as soon as new data comes in, such as rendering a search result.

tips.title: catch handles upstream errors only, and onCompletion always runs
tips.content:
The catch operator handles exceptions thrown by the flow above it. It does not catch an exception thrown in the collector (the collect block) or below it, which is called exception transparency: a flow must not hide errors that originate downstream.

Inside catch you can emit a fallback value or rethrow. onCompletion runs when the flow finishes normally, with an error, or when it is cancelled; its cause parameter tells you which. It is the right place to hide a loading indicator.

tips.title: retry and retryWhen re-collect a failed flow
tips.content:
retry(n) { predicate } re-runs the upstream flow from the start when it fails with an exception that matches the predicate, up to n times. retryWhen gives you the cause and the attempt number so you can wait between attempts, for example with exponential backoff.

Retry only errors that are worth retrying (a network IOException, not a parsing error), and remember that a retry re-collects the whole upstream, so any side effects in it run again. Never retry a CancellationException — it means the collector is gone.

tips.title: zip, combine and merge combine flows in different ways
tips.content:
zip pairs the nth value of one flow with the nth value of the other and completes as soon as either flow completes, so it is for values that belong together. combine emits whenever any input emits (once every input has emitted at least once), using the latest value of each, which suits UI state built from several sources. merge interleaves values of the same type from several flows into one, with no pairing.

Pick by the question you are asking: "these belong together" (zip), "the latest of each" (combine), "all events from any of them" (merge).
tips.codeSnippet:
val temperature = flowOf(20, 21, 22)
val label = flowOf("mon", "tue")

temperature.zip(label) { t, l -> "$l: $t" }        // "mon: 20", "tue: 21" then completes

combine(userFlow, settingsFlow) { user, settings ->
    UiState(user, settings.darkMode)               // latest user + latest settings
}

merge(clicks, keyPresses)                          // every event from either source

tips.title: flatMapConcat, flatMapMerge and flatMapLatest differ in concurrency
tips.content:
All three turn each upstream value into an inner flow and flatten the results, but they treat overlapping inner flows differently. flatMapConcat runs them one at a time, in order. flatMapMerge runs them concurrently (up to a limit, 16 by default) and emits in whichever order values arrive. flatMapLatest cancels the previous inner flow as soon as a new upstream value arrives.

Use flatMapLatest for search-as-you-type where old results are useless, flatMapConcat when order matters and each step depends on the last, and flatMapMerge to fan out independent work. Some of these operators require an opt-in annotation depending on the coroutines version.
tips.codeSnippet:
queries
    .debounce(300)
    .flatMapLatest { q -> repository.search(q) }        // cancels the stale search

ids.flatMapConcat { id -> repository.load(id) }          // strictly one after another
ids.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 4) { id -> repository.load(id) } // up to 4 at once

tips.title: Wrap callback APIs with callbackFlow, and always call awaitClose
tips.content:
callbackFlow turns a listener-based API into a Flow. Register the listener inside the block, send values with trySend, and finish with awaitClose { } to unregister. awaitClose suspends until the collector cancels or the channel closes; without it the block would end immediately and the flow would fail with an IllegalStateException.

Anything you register must be removed inside awaitClose, or the listener leaks after the collector is gone. trySend never suspends, so add buffer() or conflate() downstream if the source can produce faster than the collector consumes.

tips.title: channelFlow lets several coroutines emit into one flow
tips.content:
A flow { } builder is sequential: you can only emit from the coroutine running the block, and emitting from another coroutine throws. channelFlow is backed by a channel, so you can launch child coroutines inside it and call send from each one, which makes it the right builder for concurrent producers.

Use it to run several requests in parallel and stream results as each one finishes, instead of waiting for all of them. The flow completes when the block and all of its children are done.

tips.title: stateIn and shareIn turn a cold flow into a hot one
tips.content:
A cold flow restarts for every collector, so two screens observing the same database query run it twice. stateIn converts it into a StateFlow (with an initial value) and shareIn into a SharedFlow, both running the upstream once in a scope you provide and sharing the result.

The SharingStarted policy decides when the upstream runs. WhileSubscribed(5_000) is the common choice for UI state: it stops the upstream 5 seconds after the last collector leaves, long enough to survive a configuration change without restarting, and short enough not to keep working in the background.

tips.title: Deliver one-shot UI events with a Channel, not a SharedFlow
tips.content:
One-shot events (show a snackbar, navigate) must be handled exactly once. A MutableSharedFlow with the default replay = 0 drops an event that is emitted while nobody is collecting — for instance during a configuration change or before the screen starts collecting. A StateFlow holding the event is worse: it replays it again after rotation.

A Channel exposed with receiveAsFlow buffers events until a collector is ready and delivers each one to a single collector. Use Channel.BUFFERED so send doesn't suspend, and collect it in the UI only while it is visible.
